overview: Yum! Brands is one of the world's largest restaurant franchisors, operating a nearly all-franchised global system of more than 61,000 KFC, Taco Bell, and Pizza Hut (and Habit Burger & Grill) restaurants across roughly 155+ countries. The company closed the sale of its Pizza Hut business in 2026 (Mainland China to Yum China, the rest of the world to private equity firm LongRange Capital), narrowing its portfolio to KFC, Taco Bell, and the smaller Habit Burger & Grill chain. Yum generates the large majority of its profit from franchise and licensing royalties and fees rather than restaurant operations, making it a capital-light, high-margin, free-cash-flow-generative business.

business_model.summary: Yum earns royalties (typically 4-6% of franchisee gross sales) and franchise/development fees from a system that is approximately 98% franchised, supplemented by company-owned restaurant sales and advertising fund contributions. Revenue is overwhelmingly recurring (royalty streams tied to franchisee system sales) rather than project-based, though new-unit development and refranchising activity create episodic fee income. The post-Pizza-Hut-divestiture portfolio is concentrated in KFC (largest international/China-adjacent footprint via franchise, strong in emerging markets) and Taco Bell (the primary U.S. growth engine, nearly all domestic, low international penetration but a key expansion target).

revenue_streams.name: Franchise advertising/other services revenue (contributions to ad funds)

business_model.customer_type: B2B (franchisees who operate restaurants under license) with ultimate B2C exposure through consumer demand at the restaurant level
business_model.geographic_mix: U.S. roughly 35-40% of system sales (Taco Bell is almost entirely U.S.); KFC international (particularly emerging markets, Africa, Middle East, Latin America, and markets outside Mainland China) is the largest non-U.S. contributor; Yum divested its China Pizza Hut business to Yum China in August 2026, further reducing direct China exposure (KFC China itself was already spun off to Yum China in 2016).

competitive_position.market_position: Yum is one of the top global restaurant franchisors by unit count (60,000+ locations) with roughly a high-single-digit percent share of the fragmented global QSR market; Taco Bell is the clear U.S. share leader in Mexican-style QSR, KFC is a top-3 global chicken QSR brand, and Pizza Hut (now divested) had been losing share to Domino's.

moat_factors.description: 60,000+ unit global footprint gives purchasing power, brand reach, and development capital access that smaller franchisors cannot match
KFC and Taco Bell are top-of-mind category leaders (chicken and Mexican-style QSR respectively) with decades of consumer recognition
Asset-light royalty model generates high incremental margins and strong free cash flow relative to invested capital, funding buybacks/dividends

Proprietary AI-enabled ordering, personalization, and loyalty platform now covers the majority of system sales digitally (~60%+ digital mix), improving franchisee economics and customer data capture, though competitors are investing similarly
Long-standing, well-capitalized franchisee base supports consistent unit growth, especially in KFC's international markets

weaknesses: Post-divestiture reliance on just two major brands (KFC, Taco Bell) increases concentration risk versus a more diversified three-brand portfolio
Taco Bell is heavily U.S.-concentrated with limited international scale relative to KFC, constraining near-term diversification of that brand's growth
KFC has faced multi-year same-store sales softness and market share pressure in several markets from chicken-focused competitors and value-oriented challengers
Franchisee-dependent model limits direct control over execution, food safety, and customer experience at the restaurant level (as the 2026 cyclospora outbreak illustrated)
Limited pricing power versus value-focused consumers amid a stretched lower-income QSR customer base

growth_drivers: Continued global unit growth (targeting ~5% net new unit growth annually), with KFC and Taco Bell international expansion as the primary vehicles post-Pizza Hut sale
Scaling of the Byte by Yum! AI-enabled digital/loyalty platform across more markets and brands to lift digital mix (already ~60%+ of system sales) and same-store sales via personalization

Taco Bell U.S. same-store sales momentum (several consecutive quarters of mid-to-high single digit/even 7-9% growth in 2026) from value platforms, limited-time offers (e.g., Cantina/Live Mas Cafe initiatives), and breakfast/late-night dayparts
KFC turnaround efforts in core and emerging markets, with loyalty program rollout targeting ~75% of system sales coverage ex-China by year-end 2026
Capital redeployment of ~$2.3 billion in net Pizza Hut divestiture proceeds toward share buybacks, debt reduction, and/or reinvestment in the remaining higher-growth KFC/Taco Bell brands
Long-term algorithm target of at least 8% core operating profit growth annually, supported by a leaner, faster-growing two-brand portfolio

business.description: With Pizza Hut divested, Yum's results are now driven almost entirely by KFC and Taco Bell performance, removing a diversification buffer

business.risk: Taco Bell food safety / cyclospora outbreak
business.description: A 2026 multistate cyclospora outbreak linked to shredded lettuce at Taco Bell locations resulted in thousands of CDC-tracked illnesses, an estimated ~$20 million operating profit hit, multiple lawsuits against Taco Bell/Taylor Farms/franchisees, and some evidence of lingering Q3 2026 revenue softness from consumer caution

business.risk: KFC same-store sales softness in select markets
business.description: KFC has underperformed Taco Bell in comparable sales growth in recent quarters, with pockets of international market share loss to competitors
An almost entirely franchised model means Yum depends on franchisee capital adequacy, operational consistency, and willingness to invest in remodels/new units

financial.description: Yum carries substantial net debt (total debt ~$11.9-12.3B against modest cash) and negative shareholders' equity from years of debt-funded buybacks, elevating financial risk if cash flow or refinancing conditions deteriorate; net debt/EBITDA around 4x
A leveraged balance sheet makes refinancing costs sensitive to prevailing interest rates
International royalty streams (KFC) are exposed to foreign exchange translation into USD-reported results

regulatory.description: The cyclospora outbreak lawsuits (Ohio federal court and others) could result in settlements, reputational damage, and increased compliance/supply-chain costs
Evolving joint-employer and franchise disclosure rules in the U.S. and other markets could increase compliance costs or legal exposure
The Pizza Hut divestiture required regulatory approvals across multiple jurisdictions, a template risk for any future portfolio moves

macro.description: Value-conscious, lower-income QSR consumers are sensitive to inflation and broader economic softness, pressuring traffic and necessitating discounting
Chicken, beef, dairy, and labor cost inflation pressures franchisee margins and can indirectly affect royalty growth and system health
KFC's broad international footprint (Middle East, Africa, Latin America, emerging Asia) exposes system sales to localized boycotts, currency crises, or political instability

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Global QSR industry growth is moderate (low-to-mid single digit system sales growth) but structurally resilient, with continued share gains for value-oriented and digitally enabled chains; fast-casual competitors (Chipotle, Cava) are taking share from traditional QSR in some categories, intensifying competitive pressure on Pizza Hut-style and traditional burger/chicken formats.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate - QSR is more resilient than full-service dining in downturns due to value positioning, but still exposed to consumer discretionary spending cycles, especially among lower-income consumers who overindex at Taco Bell/KFC
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate-to-high given elevated leverage; rate changes affect refinancing costs and the relative attractiveness of Yum's dividend yield/buyback-driven capital return story

recent_developments.event: Completed sale of Pizza Hut Mainland China business to Yum China Holdings for approximately $1.2 billion; LongRange Capital's acquisition of Pizza Hut ex-China (~$1.5 billion) closed around the same time, completing Yum's exit from the Pizza Hut brand and narrowing the portfolio to KFC, Taco Bell, and Habit Burger & Grill

Reported Q2 2026 results: revenue up 12% YoY to ~$2.17 billion (slightly below consensus), adjusted EPS of $1.62 beating the $1.58 consensus; Taco Bell same-store sales +7% with 9% U.S. system sales growth; KFC same-store sales +2% with China (KFC, via Yum China) system sales +6%; Pizza Hut same-store sales -1% ahead of its divestiture

Multistate cyclospora outbreak linked to Taco Bell shredded lettuce (sourced from Taylor Farms) resulted in CDC-confirmed cases climbing into the thousands across multiple states; estimated ~$20 million Q2 operating profit hit and multiple product-liability lawsuits filed against Taco Bell, Taylor Farms, and a franchisee operator; management flagged some residual Q3 revenue softness tied to consumer caution
Reported Q1 2026 results with Taco Bell same-store sales growth of approximately 8% and core operating profit growth of roughly 10%, a strong start to the year ahead of the Pizza Hut divestiture
Leadership transition completed: former CFO and Chief Franchise Officer Chris Turner became CEO, succeeding David Gibbs (36-year Yum veteran), who remains an adviser through the end of 2026

Sell-side reaction mixed following the Pizza Hut divestiture and cyclospora fallout: JPMorgan maintained Overweight but cut its price target from $160 to $150 (late September); Baird maintained Outperform but lowered its target to $165; Argus maintained Buy while trimming its target to $180 from $185, citing a more measured growth outlook for the leaner two-brand portfolio

items.period: long-term algorithm (annual average), reaffirmed for FY2026
items.notes: Long-standing Yum growth algorithm reiterated post-Pizza Hut divestiture; management indicated the leaner KFC/Taco Bell portfolio should be able to sustain or improve on this target over time
Primarily driven by KFC international development and Taco Bell U.S./international expansion
Combines unit growth and same-store sales growth across the remaining KFC/Taco Bell/Habit portfolio

items.metric: Net proceeds from Pizza Hut divestiture
items.target: ~$2.3 billion after tax/fees (excl. up to $75 million earn-out through 2030)
items.notes: Management signaled intent to redeploy proceeds toward share repurchases, debt reduction, and/or reinvestment in KFC and Taco Bell growth

items.target: digital mix in the 60%+ range, continuing to climb (was ~63% in Q1 2026)
items.notes: Powered by the Byte by Yum! AI platform rollout and expanding loyalty program coverage (targeting ~75% of KFC system sales ex-China with loyalty coverage by year-end 2026)

guidance.management_commentary: New CEO Chris Turner and CFO leadership framed the Pizza Hut divestiture as sharpening focus on the two highest-growth, highest-return brands (KFC and Taco Bell), while reiterating the long-term 'at least 8% core operating profit growth' algorithm. Management acknowledged the cyclospora outbreak created a one-time ~$20 million Q2 profit headwind at Taco Bell and some residual Q3 revenue softness from cautious consumers, but expressed confidence the brand's value and innovation pipeline (Cantina/value platforms) would sustain its multi-quarter same-store sales momentum. Commentary also emphasized continued scaling of the Byte by Yum! digital/AI platform and loyalty programs as key margin and same-store sales levers going forward.

bull_case: Sharper, leaner two-brand portfolio (KFC, Taco Bell) after the Pizza Hut divestiture concentrates capital and management attention on the highest-growth, highest-return segments of the business
Taco Bell has been the standout performer with multiple quarters of mid-to-high single digit (even 7-9%) U.S. same-store sales growth, demonstrating pricing power and value positioning resilience
~$2.3 billion in net divestiture proceeds provides capital optionality for buybacks, debt paydown, or reinvestment, potentially accelerating EPS growth
Asset-light, nearly fully franchised royalty model continues to generate high-margin, recurring free cash flow supporting dividends (increased in Q4 2025) and buybacks

Continued digital/loyalty platform scaling (Byte by Yum!, ~60%+ digital mix) should support same-store sales and franchisee profitability, reinforcing the long-term 8%+ core operating profit algorithm
bear_case: Brand concentration risk has materially increased: with Pizza Hut gone, nearly all of Yum's profit now rides on just KFC and Taco Bell performance, removing a diversification buffer

The 2026 Taco Bell cyclospora outbreak caused real financial damage (~$20 million Q2 profit hit, thousands of illnesses, multiple lawsuits) and raises ongoing food-safety/reputational risk in a franchisee-dependent supply chain Yum does not fully control
KFC same-store sales growth continues to lag Taco Bell and faces competitive and market-specific share pressure internationally
High leverage (negative book equity, net debt/EBITDA near 4x) leaves limited balance sheet flexibility if a downturn or refinancing environment worsens
Sell-side price target cuts in September 2026 (JPMorgan, Baird) despite maintained bullish ratings suggest moderating confidence in near-term upside after the divestiture and outbreak-related noise
